religion: Christianity (Ethiopian Orthodox tradition from c.330 CE)
description: The Aksumite Empire (c.100–940 CE) was a major trading power on the horn of Africa, controlling the Red Sea coast and projecting influence into Yemen during the 6th century. Aksum was one of the first states to adopt Christianity (under King Ezana, c.330 CE), later than Armenia but earlier than the Roman Empire's general conversion. The kingdom minted its own gold, silver, and bronze coinage, extremely rare for sub-Saharan Africa, and Aksumite stelae remain among the largest single-stone monuments ever erected. Trade flowed through the port of Adulis, linking the Indian Ocean spice trade to Mediterranean buyers. The empire's decline coincided with the rise of Arab/Umayyad maritime dominance after the 7th century, which choked Adulis. Successor Christian kingdoms (Zagwe, later the Solomonic dynasty) inherited the Ge'ez language and the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition Aksum had founded.

internal_structure.legitimacy_basis: divine kingship; after 330 CE Christian anointment
internal_structure.administrative_system: subordinate sub-kings (nagasi) under a single negus negast (king of kings)

lifecycle_phases.description: Unification of pre-Aksumite chiefdoms under one royal line.
Christianization under Ezana, gold coinage, Yemen invasion under Kaleb.
Loss of Yemeni territory; Red Sea trade choked by Arab fleets.
Capital shifts inland; political authority dissolves into Zagwe successor.

rise_factors.description: Port of Adulis dominated Red Sea trade between Roman/Byzantine buyers and Indian Ocean producers.
Ezana's conversion c.330 CE allied Aksum diplomatically with Byzantine Constantinople.
Kaleb's 525 CE invasion of Himyarite Yemen demonstrated cross-Red-Sea power projection.

decline_factors.description: Umayyad/Arab maritime dominance after 640s diverted Indian Ocean trade away from Adulis.
Centuries of plough agriculture on Tigrayan highlands eroded soils, reducing surplus.
Beja and Agaw raids on the northern frontier strained the late-period army.

key_figures.name: Kaleb
key_figures.notes: Invaded Yemen to protect Christian Himyarites.
